\textbf{2. Solve quadratics over the complex numbers}\par Solve \(x^2+3x+5=0\).
\textbf{3. Solve cubic and quartic equations}\par Given \(-2+i\) is a root of \(x^3+3x^2+x-5=0\), determine the other roots.

transcription.tex: The quadratic formula\[x=\frac{-b\pm\sqrt{b^2-4ac}}{2a}\]\par has no real value when the discriminant is negative. Introducing \(i\), with \(i^2=-1\), lets us express these roots.
Complex numbers arose in sixteenth-century work on polynomial equations, including Cardano’s work.

shapes.alt: Portrait of Girolamo Cardano, introduced in the history of complex numbers.

transcription.tex: \(i=\sqrt{-1}\).\par An imaginary number has form \(bi\), \(b\in\mathbb R\), such as \(i,3i,-2i,\pi i\).\par A complex number has form \(a+bi\), \(a,b\in\mathbb R\), such as \(1+i,3-2i\). Its real part is \(a\) and its imaginary part is \(b\).

\textbf{Notation}\par Coefficients usually precede constants and variables, as in \(2\pi x\) or \(3\pi ix\). Both \(a+bi\) and \(a+ib\) are valid: multiplication commutes.\par The conventional form of Euler’s formula is \(e^{i\theta}=\cos\theta+i\sin\theta\), with special case \(e^{i\pi}+1=0\). Writing \(e^{\theta i}\) is mathematically equivalent.

transcription.tex: \textbf{1. Fractals}\par The Mandelbrot set is a famous fractal. We will investigate its recurrence later in this chapter.

transcription.tex: \textbf{2. Analytic number theory}\par Number theory studies integers. Analytic methods use real and complex variables; for example, the Riemann zeta function accepts complex inputs and is linked to the distribution of primes.
\textbf{3. Physics and engineering}\par Applications include signal analysis, quantum mechanics, fluid dynamics, relativity and control theory.

transcription.tex: \textbf{How does the Mandelbrot set work?}\par Recurrences: \(x_{n+1}=x_n+2,x_1=0\) gives \(0,2,4,\ldots\), diverging.\par \(x_{n+1}=5+x_n/2,x_1=0\) gives \(0,5,7.5,8.75,\ldots\), converging to 10.\par For the Mandelbrot set, use\[z_{n+1}=z_n^2+c,\quad z_1=0.\]

shapes.alt: Mandelbrot set on the complex plane. The filled section represents parameters whose iterates stay bounded; real axis horizontal and imaginary axis vertical.

transcription.tex: Plot \(a+bi\) at \((a,b)\) on an Argand diagram (chapter 2). The Mandelbrot set consists of the values of \(c\) whose sequence stays bounded. Bounded sequences need not converge or repeat.\par Thus \(i\), plotted at \((0,1)\), belongs to the set; 1, at \((1,0)\), does not.
Considering every \(c\) produces the fractal boundary. Colours outside the set can show escape speed; black indicates bounded behaviour in this illustration.

shapes.alt: Enlargement of the boundary: black islands sit beside alternating blue and gold spiral bands. Colour distinguishes different escape times.

transcription.tex: \(x^2+4x-5=0\) factors as \((x+5)(x-1)=0\), so its roots are \(-5,1\). Conversely, those roots give the two factors by the factor theorem.
If \(\alpha,\beta\) are the roots, the monic quadratic is\[(x-\alpha)(x-\beta)=x^2-(\alpha+\beta)x+\alpha\beta.\]
For a polynomial with real coefficients, non-real roots occur in complex conjugate pairs.\par If a real-coefficient quadratic has root \(3+4i\), what is its other root?

The non-real condition matters: two real roots need not be equal.

slides.title: Why Non-real Roots Come in Conjugate Pairs

transcription.tex: Prove that complex roots of a quadratic, with real coefficients, come in complex conjugates.

For real \(a,b,c\), \(a\ne0\), suppose \(b^2-4ac<0\).\[z=\frac{-b\pm\sqrt{b^2-4ac}}{2a}\]\[=-\frac b{2a}\pm\frac{\sqrt{b^2-4ac}}{2a}\]\[=-\frac b{2a}\pm\frac{\sqrt{4ac-b^2}}{2a}i.\]\par The real parts are equal and imaginary parts opposite: the roots are conjugates.

\(\alpha+\beta\) and \(\alpha\beta\) must be real. Put \(\alpha=a_1+b_1i,\beta=a_2+b_2i\).\par \(\alpha+\beta=(a_1+a_2)+(b_1+b_2)i\). From the sum, \(b_1+b_2=0\), so \(b_2=-b_1\).\[\alpha\beta=(a_1a_2-b_1b_2)+(a_1b_2+a_2b_1)i.\]\par Its imaginary part vanishes:\[-a_1b_1+a_2b_1=b_1(a_2-a_1)=0.\]\par Either \(b_1=b_2=0\) (both roots real), or \(a_2=a_1\) and \(b_2=-b_1\), proving conjugacy for non-real roots.

transcription.tex: Given that \(3+i\) is a root of the quartic equation \par \(2{z}^{4}-3{z}^{3}-39{z}^{2}+120z-50=0\), solve the equation completely.
The conjugate \(3-i\) is also a root, so\[(z-(3+i))(z-(3-i))=z^2-6z+10\]\par is a factor.
You could also use algebraic long division to obtain the other factor.

The other factor starts with \(2z^2\) and ends with \(-5\). Write \(2z^2+az-5\).\par Compare the coefficient of \(z^3\): \(a-12=-3\), so \(a=9\). Expanding verifies all coefficients:\[(z^2-6z+10)(2z^2+9z-5)=0.\]

transcription.tex: $\mathrm g(z)=z^4+2z^3-z^2+38z+130$\par Given that $\mathrm g(2+3i)=0$, find all the roots of $\mathrm g(z)=0$.
1. Conjugate factor \(2-3i\) is also a root, so\[(z-(2+3i))(z-(2-3i))=z^2-4z+13\]\par is a factor.
2. Divide Division steps:\[g(z)-z^2(z^2-4z+13)=6z^3-14z^2+38z+130.\]\par Subtract \(6z(z^2-4z+13)\) to leave \(10z^2-40z+130\), which is \(10(z^2-4z+13)\).\par Hence the quotient is \(z^2+6z+10\).
3. Roots \[g(z)=(z^2-4z+13)(z^2+6z+10).\]\par The first factor gives \(2\pm3i\). For the second,\[(z+3)^2=-1\Rightarrow z=-3\pm i.\]\par All four roots are \(2+3i,2-3i,-3+i,-3-i\).

transcription.tex: $\mathrm f(z)=z^4-10z^3+71z^2+Qz+442$, where $Q$ is a real constant.\par Given that $z=2-3i$ is a root of the equation $\mathrm f(z)=0$,\par (a) show that $z^2-6z+34$ is a factor of $\mathrm f(z)$\par (b) find the value of $Q$\par (c) solve completely the equation $\mathrm f(z)=0$.

(a) \(2+3i\) is also a root, so \(z^2-4z+13\) is a factor. Write\[f(z)=(z^2-4z+13)(z^2+bz+c).\]\par Constant terms: \(13c=442\Rightarrow c=34\). Cubic terms: \(b-4=-10\Rightarrow b=-6\). The quadratic coefficient is \(34+24+13=71\), as required. Thus the other factor is \(z^2-6z+34\).
(c) \[f(z)=(z^2-4z+13)(z^2-6z+34).\]\par The first factor gives \(2\pm3i\). The second gives \((z-3)^2=-25\), hence \(3\pm5i\).
